title: Glycogen Metabolism
objectives: Understand the processes of glycogenesis and glycogenolysis
Identify key enzymes involved in glycogen metabolism
Explain the regulation of glycogen synthesis and breakdown
Recognize clinical implications of glycogen metabolism disorders

overview.title: Pathway Overview
overview.content:
Glycogen Metabolism Overview

Glycogen metabolism consists of two opposing pathways: glycogenesis (synthesis of glycogen from glucose) and glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate).

Glycogen serves as the main storage form of glucose in animal cells, primarily in liver and skeletal muscles, with smaller amounts in brain and adipose tissue.

  • Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose levels between meals
  • Muscle glycogen provides immediate energy for muscle contraction
  • Brain glycogen serves as an emergency energy reserve

glycogenesis.title: Glycogenesis
glycogenesis.content:
Glycogenesis

Pathway for synthesis of glycogen from glucose. Substrate is glucose 6-P. Occurs in the cytosol in virtually all animal tissues, mainly in liver & skeletal muscles.

Four Stages of Glycogenesis

1. Synthesis of UDP-glucose

Steps: Glucose → glucose 6-P (hexokinase/glucokinase) → glucose 1-P (phosphoglucomutase) → UDP-glucose (UDP-glucose phosphorylase)

Note: UDP-glucose is the immediate donor of glucose residues and also involved in lactose synthesis.

2. Synthesis of Glycogen Primer

Process: First glucose attaches to Tyr194 of glycogenin via intrinsic glucosyl transferase activity, followed by addition of 7 more glucose residues.

3. Elongation of Glycogen Chain

Enzyme: Glycogen synthase (committed step)

Action: Transfers glucose residues to non-reducing ends forming α-1,4 glycosidic bonds

4. Branching

Enzyme: Branching enzyme (amylose α1,4→α1,6 transglucosidase)

Action: Transfers 6-8 glucose residues to form α-1,6 linkages when chain reaches 11+ residues

glycogenolysis.title: Glycogenolysis
glycogenolysis.content:
Glycogenolysis

Pathway for phosphorolytic breakdown of glycogen into glucose 1-P & glucose. Occurs mainly in liver & muscle cytosol (also in lysosomes).

Four Steps of Glycogenolysis

1. Chain Shortening

Enzyme: Glycogen phosphorylase (committed step, requires pyridoxal phosphate)

Action: Removes terminal glucose residues as glucose 1-P until limit dextrin (4 residues before branch point)

2. Debranching

Enzyme: Debranching enzyme (two domains: glucan transferase and amylose 1,6 glucosidase)

Action: Transfers trisaccharide units and hydrolyzes α-1,6 linkages

3. Further Processing

Alternating action of phosphorylase and debranching enzyme continues degradation

4. Isomerization

Enzyme: Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose 1-P to glucose 6-P

Tissue-Specific Fate of Glucose 6-P

Liver/Kidney: Converted to free glucose via glucose-6-phosphatase

Muscle/Adipose: Enters glycolysis (lack glucose-6-phosphatase)

regulation.title: Regulation
regulation.content:
Regulation of Glycogen Metabolism

Glycogenesis and glycogenolysis are reciprocally regulated through allosteric mechanisms and covalent modification of key enzymes.

Covalent Modification

Phosphorylation: Inhibits glycogen synthase (GS) and activates glycogen phosphorylase (GP) - favors glycogenolysis

Dephosphorylation: Activates GS and inhibits GP - favors glycogenesis

Hormonal Control

Insulin: Activates GS via PKB-mediated inhibition of GSK3

Glucagon/Epinephrine: Activate GP via cAMP-dependent protein kinase

Calcium (muscle): Activates GP kinase during contraction

Allosteric Regulation

Glucose 6-P activates PP1 which dephosphorylates GS

AMP activates GP in muscle during energy deficit

clinical.title: Clinical Notes
clinical.content:
Clinical Correlations

Glycogen Storage Diseases

Various inherited disorders affecting glycogen metabolism enzymes:

Type I (von Gierke): Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency - severe fasting hypoglycemia

Type II (Pompe): Lysosomal acid maltase deficiency - cardiomyopathy

Type III (Cori): Debranching enzyme deficiency - hepatomegaly

Type V (McArdle): Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency - exercise intolerance

Diagnosis:

Enzyme assays, genetic testing, and clinical presentation evaluation

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why can't muscle glycogen contribute directly to blood glucose?
A: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-P from glycogenolysis can only enter glycolysis locally, not be released as free glucose.
Q: How does insulin promote glycogen synthesis?
A: Insulin activates protein kinase B (PKB) which phosphorylates and inactivates GSK3, preventing its inhibition of glycogen synthase.
Q: What is the advantage of glycogen's branched structure?
A: Branching increases solubility and provides more non-reducing ends for simultaneous synthesis/degradation, allowing rapid glucose mobilization.
